explanations.explanation: This feature is responding to the Python-style exponentiation operator “**” in code-like math expressions (e.g. n**2, b**3, x**3 + 6*x**2, etc.).

This feature flags the opening token of a new content block (headline, label or section header) in news/blog/forum text—e.g. “Video,” “The…,” “News,” dates, “Exclusive,” “5 Best Tips,” etc.—marking the start of an article or section.

This feature fire­s on “structural” tokens—the closed-class words (auxiliary verbs like be/was, negation particles ’t/not, prepositions like of/to, conjunctions/conditionals like if/there/continue) and punctuation or delimiters (slashes, commas, braces, equals signs)—i.e. the grammatical or code-syntax scaffolding rather than content words.
This feature turns on whenever the model sees the double‐asterisk markers (“**”) used to open or close bold text—typically bracketing headings or titles in markdown.

This neuron is a discourse‐structure detector—it lights up on clause or sentence-initial function words (prepositional heads like “at,” “with,” “by,” “for,” the relative pronoun “which,” quantifier phrases “at least,” and even first-person markers “we/our”) that commonly introduce or frame propositions in academic writing.

This feature fires on the little “glue” tokens and keywords that tie names to values or definitions across code, data and prose—for example import markers (“use”), equality/assignment operators (`==`, `===`, `=`), key-value separators (`:`, `->`), step dashes or list bullets, string‐concatenation pluses, and section-intro words (“As,” “Design”) that all serve to declare, assign or map one thing to another.

This feature flags the start‐of‐block “title” or heading token across domains—e.g. article headlines, class or manifest declarations, XML/HTML/PHP entry points, CTAs (“Register Now,” “Connect with us”), section headings, etc.

This neuron fires on the “last item” in any small structured list or table-like block—be it the final timestamp in a CSV filter, the last ingredient in a recipe, the last cast member in a film infobox, the bottom row of a ratings table, the final case in code, the last entry in an icons list, etc. It thus marks the concluding element of enumerations or tabular sections.

This neuron fires on subordinating discourse markers—words like “because,” “since,” “if,” “while,” etc.—that introduce causal, conditional or concessive subordinate clauses, signaling the logical/contrastive link between two parts of a sentence.

This feature fires on the last word or punctuation of standalone headings/titles (e.g. headlines, section titles, metadata lines) across diverse text, marking the boundary between a header and the following body.

1. “mean” as a definition marker: signals an explicit explanation of a term’s meaning.  
2. “Look at” as an attention directive: points the reader to a specific location or element.  
3. “answer is:” as a solution label: introduces the definitive response to a question.  
4. “Many believe” as a common‐belief introducer: flags a widely held opinion or misconception.  
5. “One is” as an option enumerator: marks the first of multiple methods or choices.  
6. “see” as an observation verb: reports an observed statistic or phenomenon.  
7. “was” as a copular definitional link: ties a subject to its description or definition.  
8. “use” as an imperative instruction: directs how to apply a feature or command.  
9. “involves” as a definition‐building verb: outlines key components of a concept.  
10. “use” as a mechanism descriptor: explains how a process employs a technique.  
11. (reuse of “Look at”) same attention‐directing function as item 2.  
12. “catch:” as a caveat introducer: signals an exception or essential condition.  
13. “means” as an etymology/definition introducer: explains the literal meaning of a name or term.  
14. “premise:” as a scenario‐summarizing label: introduces the core setup of a narrative or problem.  
15. “is” in “first function is”: links a listed function to its description in technical writing.  
16. “says” as an attribution verb: cites documentation or an authority as source.  
17. “see” as a perception verb: indicates stakeholders’ view or interpretation of something.  
18. “answer:” as a concise reply introducer: precedes a brief, definitive answer.

This feature detects the “dot” punctuation that closes off abbreviations or domain-specific suffixes—e.g. month abbreviations (Sept., Nov.), honorifics/titles (St., M.D.), patent or document codes (No.), file-extensions (.js), etc.—particularly in technical or formal text.

This neuron is a “comment-start” detector in threaded forum posts: it spikes on the very first substantive word of a user’s reply (i.e. immediately after the separator or metadata), marking the boundary between header/links and the body of the comment.
This feature fires on the final content token of a self-standing sentence or heading—e.g. the last word (or its closing period) in license headers, article titles, section captions, headlines, etc.

This neuron flags the kind of front-loaded, reader-directed prompts or headings you see in forums and help pages—imperative or conditional openers (e.g. “Have Questions?”, “Meet…!”, “If this is your first visit…”) used to call readers’ attention or guide them to take action.

This neuron fires on the little “linkers” and common endings in scientific/medical jargon—hyphens and suffix fragments that join or terminate technical abbreviations and compound names (e.g. the “-” in CK-MB or IGF-I, the “RH” in GnRH, the “-density” in high-density, enzyme/receptor suffixes like “-ase” or “-lact,” measurement digits, etc.). It effectively flags subword boundaries and standardized affixes in domain-specific nomenclature.

explanations.explanation: This neuron seems to fire on the little “structural” or meta-linguistic cues that kick off non-narrative segments—bracketed editorial notes or stage directions ([SIC], [applause], [groans]), the first word of a quotation or answer (“People,” “You,” “I’m,” “It’s,” “Now”), byline or named‐entity markers (Marie, Mr Hammond, Cresud), and other such boundary-signaling tokens that mark speaker turns, annotations, or metadata.

This neuron marks the end‐of‐header or metadata zone—e.g. the last word or punctuation of a headline or byline, or the opening parenthesis after a Wikipedia article’s subject line—flagging the boundary just before the main body text begins.

The feature is a “heading/title‐delimiter” detector. It spikes at the end of standalone lines that serve as section or article titles (blog/nav menus, news datelines, patent headers, paper titles, software version headings, etc.), marking the boundary between a heading and the following body text.

This feature fires on the little “signpost” phrases that kick off or steer expository chunks—things like “one of the…,” “let us now look at…,” and the “we …” verbs (“we present/report/evaluate/review/conducted”). In other words, it detects discourse markers that introduce new sections, enumerate points, or announce contributions in academic, technical, or promotional prose.

This neuron fires on the break right after a high‐level label or heading—whether it’s a site/menu title (“Main menu,” “News,” “Let’s Talk,” “Donate,” “Shop by Brand,” “Follow Us,” etc.), a project/configuration tag (`<Configuration>`), or a copyright/metadata line (“Experience Inc.,” “Microsoft Corporation,” etc.). In other words, it’s signaling the end of a section heading or metadata header and the start of the following content.

This feature fires on words naming large‐scale, collective events or phenomena—wars, economic depressions, natural disasters, systemic crises or broad policy issues (e.g. “War,” “Depression,” “tsunamis,” “atrocities,” “hardship,” “global warming,” “gun control,” etc.).

This feature fires on the little “formatting” markers—chiefly the double‐asterisk ** (and related /** tokens)—that authors and UIs use to mark off headlines, section titles or comment headers from the body text.

This feature lights up on the little alphanumeric pieces and separators that encode quantitative or code‐like information in technical text—single digits in decimals, percentages or classification codes, punctuation like slashes (e.g. “mg/kg,” “mg/L”) and hyphens in compound terms, and short two-letter fragments within domain-specific names (e.g. “ul” in sulbactam, “oz” in repository, “of” in POSI).

This head‐case feature fires on tokens that are part of proper names or titles—e.g. people’s surnames, book/film or section headings, library‐module names, quoted titles, etc. It marks tokens in title‐case sequences used as named entities.

This neuron is essentially a “boundary detector” for news‐style text—it spikes at the very end of headlines or sentences (periods, closing quotes, paragraph breaks) in journalistic/blog contexts, marking where one segment ends and the next begins.
This neuron is a boundary‐marker detector—it spikes on tokens that close out a unit (most often the sentence‐final period, or the last word of a heading/title), signaling an end‐of‐segment boundary.

explanations.explanation: This neuron fires on the hyphen character when it’s being used as a connective separator in compound tokens—e.g. linking date fields (YYYY-MM-DD), CSS class modifiers (col-sm-9), chemical names (5-hydroxy-…), URL or tag fragments, and similar contexts.

This neuron fires on “boundary” tokens that end chunks of text—whether the dateline in a news story (e.g. “MAN­CHESTER,” “Nov.”), the last word of a headline or UI section title (“News,” “Search form,” “Stay in the loop”), or the final token of a sentence (the word just before the period). It thus marks the ends of sentences, headlines, and other sectional units.

This feature flags “metadata” or “preamble” text in code and config files—i.e. comment- and doc-comment markers (//, /*, ///), license-header clauses, schema/docs keywords, config keys (importHelpers), media-query hyphens, the first non‐logicals like “int rows=” etc.—all the non-functional, descriptive or declarative parts rather than algorithmic code.

This feature lights up on sentence‐ or segment‐boundary markers—full stops (and their following line breaks or capitalized next words) as well as the start of new sentences—encoding where one sentence ends and the next begins.

This feature lights up on the little “connective” punctuation (hyphens or colons) inside compound technical identifiers—e.g. the “–” in IL-6, IL-17A or TNF-α, the “:” in xml:space or xliff:document, the “-” in scanned-page—i.e. the delimiter that joins a prefix or acronym to its numeric, subtype or namespace qualifier.

This feature marks the boundary at the end of a section heading or introductory summary—e.g. the final word or punctuation that closes a patent‐style “This invention relates…” sentence or a blog/article title.

explanations.explanation: This neuron fires on “non‐lexical” tokens—short uppercase (or mixed‐case) letter sequences, numerals, and punctuation (slashes, hyphens, etc.) that typically appear in codes, acronyms, IDs, URLs, legal or technical references, and other structured/text‐markup fragments rather than ordinary words.

This neuron fires on high‐level section markers—i.e. the first word of a new heading or title (often capitalized words like “Currently,” “Don,” “See,” “Major Feature … Prime”) and the punctuation that ends those headings (the lone period after a patent title, article title, menu label, etc.). It is effectively signaling the boundaries of top-level sections or headers.

explanations.explanation: This neuron is basically a “continuation” detector – it lights up on subword pieces that occur inside a word (rather than at its start), across all scripts.
This neuron is essentially a “full‐stop” detector—it fires on the period token (.) when it’s used to end sentences or act as a dot‐separator (e.g. in URLs).

This feature fires on the “*” glyph when it’s used as a line‐prefix marker—i.e. the asterisk that introduces bullet points or comment‐continuation lines (as in license clauses, code‐comment blocks, news‐item bullets, etc.).

This feature fires on structural “glue” tokens that link or separate elements in text—most notably the preposition “of” in noun phrases, slash “/” characters in file‐path strings, and leading numerals in count/percent expressions.

This neuron is a layout‐/structure detector that lights up on block-level headings and metadata labels—things like menu titles (“Main menu,” “Services”), article or section headlines (“News,” paper titles), press-release datelines (“NEW YORK, Dec. 23 2011…”), conference names, code-section markers, etc.—i.e. the labels that signal the start of a new content section.
